cells.tense: Something here burns steady now, and it is being tended where it sits.
cells.act: persist on hope that has been tested
cells.ask: Go back to the one shared practice that still feels like yours — the meal, the walk, the song — and hold to that choice across a season of doubt, showing up whether or not it thrills you.
cells.core:
In the life you share with others, something burns steady and you're keeping it going in plain ways. You turn up, you know the words, you take your part without ceremony. What took years to build is still here because someone keeps coming back to it, and that someone is you.

Take the one shared practice that still feels like yours — the meal, the walk, the song — and hold to that choice across a season of doubt, showing up whether or not it thrills you. Nothing is coming to confirm it and nothing needs to. What's wanted is the next arrival, then the one after, chosen again once the shine is gone. That is the part that outlives the mood it started in.

cells.tense: It will be made ready for a gathering that hasn't begun yet.
cells.ask: Lay the shared thing out whole — what it's for, who it's for, every part — until nothing more about it can be seen, and let the plans wait until that is done.
cells.core:
What you share with people has turned into a project. It is becoming an event, a revival, a statement about who all of you are, worked out detail by detail for a day that hasn't arrived. Those it's meant to serve are getting a version already finished. There isn't much room left in it for anyone else to put in a hand.

Lay the shared thing out whole — what it's for, who it's for, every part — until nothing more about it can be seen, and let the plans wait until that is done. Some of what's there will turn out to be scaffolding. Seeing it complete, once, plainly, shows which parts carry weight and which are material hauled in too early.

cells.tense: It was tended once, at a table already behind you.
cells.act: name every feeling in it on one page, none of them crossed out
cells.ask: After one shared meal or ceremony this week, put down on a page every feeling that came during it, warm and awkward together, and cross nothing off.
cells.core:
What you share with others has gone quiet. You still turn up, you still know the words, you still take your part. The room you're in and the room inside you aren't the same room anymore. Habit is holding the forms up while whatever they were for sits behind a door you already walked through.

After one shared meal or ceremony this week, put down on a page every feeling that came during it, warm and awkward together, and cross nothing off. The door won't open because you push on it. It opens when everything that's there is allowed to be there, and the forms go back to holding something warm.

cells.tense: Something is lit in what you carry for others, and your account leaves you out.
cells.act: eat the meal you made and leave the kitchen as it is
cells.ask: Fix one shared thing you helped pass on — the recipe, the songs, the way your family marks a day — then sit down with it finished, changing nothing and tidying nothing after.
cells.core:
In your shared life, something runs through your hands. You remember the recipe, the songs, the way your family marks a day. When people thank the tradition, the tradition gets the credit and you get a nod. You say you only hold onto it. The room stays full because you keep filling it.

Fix one shared thing you helped pass on — the recipe, the songs, the way your family marks a day — then sit down with it finished, changing nothing and tidying nothing after. Let the completed thing sit whole in your hands for a while, yours too. What you've been carrying was carried by you, and it belongs to nobody's use more than yours.

attempts.check: The draft wants to name what the person is keeping alive or reviving — a tradition, a practice — but the record only says a spark is present in shared meaning and hasn't found its shape yet, so I cannot say what it is for or who it is for. A reader could fairly say 'I'm not starting anything; I'm just doing what we've always done,' and the cells must still be useful there — the spark may be in the carrying, not the starting. The ask survives being wrong because tending the shared thing more deliberately is good whether or not my read is right. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the one that would make the spark sound like a mandate to originate something new; I've cut it. For Too Little I located where the person stands (lapsed, half-arriving, warmed by forms whose meaning didn't take) and did not say what happened or who left, cost, or lesson.
